title: Seasonal Weight limits lifted
full_story:
Beginning Wednesday, April 8th, 2026, seasonal reduced weight limits will be suspended until further notice for all roads included in the county highway system with seasonal weight limit signs.  Weight limit restrictions may be in place on township roads.  Please contact the respective township road commissioner. Please tune to WNOI, Clay County Sheriff’s phone app or visit the Engineer/ Highway website under Offices Section of the Clay County web site at https://claycounty.illinois.gov/engineering-highway/ for load limit information.  The highway department would like to keep the roads open as much as possible.  PLEASE respect the load limits when they are in effect.  Damaging the roads with heavy loads not only costs taxpayer money but it also affects your neighbors and fellow Clay county residents.  Please be kind and respect the load limits.

title: CLAY CITY VILLAGE BOARD MEETS
full_story:
The Clay City Village Board met Tuesday evening and didn’t waste any time before delving into controversy.

Just after Mayor Mike Delonshaw called the meeting to order the first order of business was a vote to permit Trustee Beth Prosser to attend the meeting electronically, which was approved.  The board then considered passage of the past meeting minutes and the bills.  Trustee Sue Lindeman was quickly joined by fellow trustees Jim Duff and Larry Phillips who questioned invoices from Ameren.  Specifically, it was a $21,000 Ameren charge that raised concerns.  The trio struggled to understand how Ameren was billing the village while the village was using the electric aggregator Homefield.  Village Clerk Shannon Hall said Ameren was just trying to catch up, but she would contact them to better clarify the issue.  There were also questions about money paid to ServPro and to USDI.  For ServPro, it was explained that the village pays the fee to the company and is then reimbursed by insurance.  For USDI, the company was paid for the removal of old gas lines.  Lindeman stated that she thought the board decided not to have additional lines removed.  Mayor Delonshaw and Utilities Superintendent Sean Sullens said they only did a few when the company was in town.  In the end, trustees voted to approve past meeting minutes and the bills.

Dick Petrea with Leymone Hardcastle CPAs was scheduled to present the village audit, however he was unable to attend and the measure was tabled until next month’s meeting.

Next, Mayor Delonshaw stated it was time to open the bids submitted for the property at 400 S. Main St.  He stated they received just one bid.  It was submitted by Fellowship Church (formerly Clay City Methodist Church) in the amount of $7,500.  Sue Lindeman asked how much the village had in the property after taking it over and demolition and clean up.  The answer provided was $15,000.  This began a lengthy discussion about whether to accept the offer or not.  There was also talk about if the church decides to sell the property, if it wanted a stipulation in the sales contract to include language for the first right of refusal and given the opportunity to match any offer.  Church officials didn’t think that language would be an issue but needed to confer with the congregation before agreeing to those terms.  In the end, the board agreed to have Village Attorney Barry Bright draw up a minimal document stating the village position without formally accepting the bid offered.

Another protracted discussion started over how to dispense with surplus village property that Mayor Delonshaw described as pretty much junk.  The items include a dump truck, a pickup truck, a bush hog, a trench digging machine and other assorted items.  The mayor asked trustees how they wanted to get rid of the items.  Whether they should seek bids, sell it for scrap or simply dispose of it.  Attorney Bright said an ordinance had been drawn up to deal with the issue and gives the mayor permission to dispense with the items at his discretion.  The ordinance would be a general document that could handle similar situations in the future by simply filling in blanks and then voting to approve it.  Trustees Duff, Lindeman and Phillips appeared agitated with the thought of paying the attorney to create an ordinance that, in their view, wasn’t necessary.  Attorney Bright said that to sell equipment such as was being offered would be illegal, but if the board wanted to do that it would be up to them.  Trustee Travis Strasbaugh stated the issue was about transparency in the process, which Bright quickly agreed was correct.  When the discussion ended, trustees voted to approve the ordinance giving the mayor the authority to sell or dispose of the surplus equipment at his discretion.

The next item was about oiling and chipping Clay City streets.  Brandon Bridges with Charleston Engineering of Olney and the son of the late Engineer Mike Bridges presented the proposal to oil and chip village streets this year.  Bridges said he had prepared a resolution for the board’s consideration.  It allows for up to $48,000 to be used to oil and chip Clay City streets.  Following a couple of questions about the vendor supplying the oil and what grade of oil is proper, the board approved the measure without dissent.

Attorney Barry Bright then presented an ordinance that was first discussed at the March meeting on the destruction of audio tapes from past closed meeting sessions.  There was some confusion over whether board members were given the opportunity to see the transcribed verbatim minutes from those meetings, since one meeting was not originally included.  As the discussion dragged on, it was suggested the issue be dealt with in closed session where it could be freely discussed before taking any action.  So the issue was tabled until later in the meeting.

Utility Superintendent Sean Sullens brought information from a resident to the board.  He said during a sewage clog, the village sought assistance from the City of Flora.  Their equipment was able to clear the line.  However, one resident complained that the fix caused damage to his home when sewage backed up and flooded his basement and potentially caused damage to another bathroom upstairs.  Photos of the damage were presented.  Sullens didn’t think there was any way the damage cited was caused by what happened.  Trustees appeared to agree and said the owner should submit an insurance claim, which they suspected would not be successful.  Sullens also had a request of the board.  He asked for the village to purchase a wide, flat-bottom boat for use at the lagoon for maintenance or during times of flooding.  Trustees stated to try to find a used boat and trailer and they would consider it at the appropriate time.

Before the meeting moved into closed session, Clerk Shannon Hall commented that there were no transfers between funds.  There was a brief discussion about the hiring of summer help.  Trustees commented that there are three full-time and one part-time employee and there didn’t appear to be a need for a summer employee.  There was also a request for office help at village hall, but that was moved to closed session.  Mayor Delonshaw also noted that a resident wanted to be able to empty his camper’s tote tank into the village sewer line.  Following a brief discussion no action was taken.  Trustee Sue Lindeman reminded residents to please remove trash totes after they have been emptied by DBS Disposal.

The board then voted to go into closed session, the results of which were not immediately available.

title: DRUG TAKE BACK DAY
full_story:
The Clay County Hospital will be the drop off location for the Clay County prescription drug take-back initiative on Saturday, April 25th from 10 am to 1 pm.

The National Prescription Drug Take Back Day aims to provide a safe, convenient, and responsible means of disposing of prescription drugs, while also educating the general public about the potential for abuse of medications.

Unused medications in the home are a source of drug abuse in millions of homes, 80% of US waterways show traces of common medication; and 56% of teens think that prescription drugs are easier to get than illicit drugs.

The Drug Take Back Day will provide a safe and trusted method of disposal of prescription drugs.

The drug take back event on Saturday, April 25th is sponsored by the Coalition Against Drug Abuse of Clay County in cooperation with the Clay County Sheriff’s Office, Flora Police Department, Clay County Hospital, Clay County Solid Waste Committee, Clay County Health Department, and Clay County Probation.

title: MASSAGE THERAPY CLINICALS
full_story:
Olney Central College’s Massage Therapy Program is accepting appointments for Spring clinicals.

The clinics are open to the public and will be held from 9:15 am to 2 pm on Saturday, April 11th and April 24th at the West Richland Center in Noble.

The cost for a relaxing massage is $45 for an hour and $30 for half an hour.  A 20-minute chair massage is $20.

Clinics are by appointment only and can be made by calling 618-392-2430.  Callers should leave a message with their names, contact information and date desired.  Students will return phone messages during Monday and Wednesday evening classes to confirm appointments.

title: NO BODY TO MURDER
full_story:
A play titled “No Body to Murder” will be held at Nostalgia Theater, formerly the Town Theater, in downtown Flora this weekend.  The play will be held Friday, and Saturday, at 7 pm each night.  This fun whodunnit takes place on a stormy night and will have you laughing along and keep you guessing.  This is a stage performance, not a murder mystery event and there will be no audience participation.

The play is directed by Stacey Earleywine and is full of amazing local talent, who will blow you away with their acting abilities.  Although this play is not a musical, it is full of great songs in between scenes.

Grab a friend and enjoy an evening out with well-known community theater members Jeremy Kohn, Jim Earleywine, Matt Lovett, Jessica Muskopf, Linda Waller, Sarah Hager, and more.

Nostalgia Theater is currently being renovated and will serve as Clay County’s home for community theater.  Not only will you be able to catch some amazing live entertainment at Nostalgia, but the building is also for rent as a venue for upcoming events, such as parties, reunions, showers, and weddings.

Nostalgia Theater operates as a 501©3 non-profit and all proceeds from the Nostalgia play performances will be used to continue the renovation of the theater.  Make plans to attend this fun performance, support the hard work these actors have put into it, and see the beautiful Nostalgia Theater building as it is being brought back to life.

Tickets are $10 each.  Tickets are on sale Wednesday through Friday at Cuttin’ Up Hair Salon, next to Nostalgia Theater.  Tickets will also be available at the door.

Stacey Earlywine and Beth Cooper will be the guests today on The ReVue at 2 pm talking about this weekends play.

title: FLORA HIGH SCHOOL CONCERT
full_story:
The Flora High School Music Department will have their Spring Concert at 2 pm on Sunday, April 19th in the Harry Penry Auditorium.

The Concert will feature music from the Rock Band, Jazz Band, Concert Choir, and Concert Band all under the direction of Ethan Steber.  He says that all 4 groups have been working hard on their performances.  Steber said the concert band is excited to perform “The Great Rubber Chicken Gallop” by Randall Stanbridge, and the Jazz Band will perform Jo Jo Calypso by Jim Nadel among other songs.

The Concert will be at 2 pm on Sunday, April 19th in the Harry Penry Auditorium.

title: CROP PROGRESS AND CONDITION
full_story:
The first weekly crop progress and condition report of the season was issued on Monday afternoon and planting season is officially underway in some parts of the state.

According to USDA’s first weekly crop progress and condition report of the year, an estimated 1% of Illinois corn had been planted as of April 5, in line with the five-year average pace. The department expects to have soybean planting data in next week’s report.

According to the USDA there were 2.1 days suitable for fieldwork in the week ending April 5th.  Statewide, the average temperature was 59.1 degrees, 11.3 degrees above average.  Precipitation averaged 2.23 inches, 1.53 inches above normal.  Topsoil moisture supply was rated 5% very short, 16% short, 62% adequate, and 17% surplus.  Subsoil moisture supply was rated 15% very short, 29% short, 51% adequate, and 5% surplus.

Winter wheat condition was rated 1% very poor, 3% poor, 24% fair, 62% good, and 10% excellent.

title: GET COVERED IL ENROLLMENT
full_story:
Open enrollment has ended, but uninsured Illinoisans can still enroll in a health insurance plan through the state’s new Tax Time Easy Enrollment program.  The program provides a pathway to coverage for residents as part of the annual tax filing process.  With the deadline to file taxes approaching on April 15th, Get Covered Illinois is encouraging filers to take advantage of this new program.

When completing their IL-1040, residents seeking coverage should check the Health Insurance box on line 42 and indicate which household members need insurance.  The Illinois Department of Revenue will share information about the household, such as income and household size, with Get Covered Illinois.  Filers will receive a notice from Get Covered Illinois outlining their projected eligibility for health coverage, including potential qualification for premium tax credits or Medicaid.  If eligible for Marketplace insurance, the customer has 60 days from the date on the notice to apply and enroll in a health plan.  Checking the box does not affect the filer’s tax return and does not require any commitment to enroll in coverage.

“By embedding health insurance enrollment into the annual tax filing process, Illinois is making it easier than ever for residents to take the first step toward getting covered,” said Get Covered Illinois Director Morgan Winters.  “As a state-based marketplace, we now have the ability to create programs like Tax Time Easy Enrollment that open new pathways to coverage for our residents.

Residents who experience a life change like loss of health coverage, marriage, or the birth of a child may also qualify for a special enrollment period.  This year, Get Covered Illinois added pregnancy as a qualifying life event.  “Illinois continues to expand access to coverage by aligning enrollment with the real-life moments when people need care,” said Director Winters.  “By recognizing pregnancy as a qualifying life event, we’re making it easier for Illinoisans to enroll in coverage when they need it most.”

For more information and to apply for coverage, residents can visit GetCoveredIllinois.gov/SpecialEnrollment or connect with a certified broker or navigator who can provide free enrollment assistance.

title: CHICKEN NUGGET RECALL
full_story:
Food safety officials are warning the public to not eat certain frozen chicken nuggets after tests found dangerous levels of lead.

The US Department of Agriculture and Inspection Service issued a public health alert for dinosaur shaped, ready-to-eat chicken nuggets sold under the Great Value brand at Walmart.  A recall was not issued because the nuggets are no longer being sold, but officials say some may still be in people’s freezers.

The alert applies to 29-ounce bags of “Great Value fully cooked dino shaped chicken breast nuggets” with a best if used by date of February 10th, 2027.  The USDA said the nuggets were produced on February 10th and shipped to Walmart stores nationally.
